news_posts.post_content:
Always let AI surface performance anomalies before they affect users.

When you set up monitoring, let the tool analyze query latency,
 memory usage,
 connection spikes,
 and error rates in real time.

Opvizor just announced a platform that does exactly that for MongoDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Redis, and SQL Server.

The service combines continuous metrics collection with machine‑learning models that flag outliers without you writing custom rules.

For a data engineer, that means you can spend less time writing dashboards and more time fixing the root cause.

A practical tip: integrate the AI alerts with your incident channel,
 and treat the first alert as a clue, not a fire.

If the model highlights a sudden increase in lock wait time on PostgreSQL,
 investigate recent schema changes before scaling hardware.

Similarly, a spike in cache miss rate on Redis may point to a bad eviction policy rather than needing a larger node.

The key benefit is faster triage and fewer false alarms,
 because the model learns the normal baseline for each database instance.

Give the free trial a run,
 set a few baseline alerts,
 and let the AI suggest the next steps.

You’ll quickly see how proactive diagnostics keep your pipelines humming.

news_posts.post_content:
Imagine you’re pulling a sales report in the middle of the day.

You need the latest transaction data,
and the same query also powers a dashboard.

In the past you’d run the report against a data warehouse,
then run a separate OLTP query against the source.

That split adds latency,
and extra ETL work.

Now Microsoft is adding a serverless PostgreSQL layer inside Fabric.

It lets you run transactional queries and analytical queries in the same environment.

The contrast is clear: you either manage two systems,
or you let Fabric handle both.

For a data engineer this means fewer pipelines to maintain.

You can write a single SQL query that reads fresh rows and feeds a chart without moving data.

Because it’s serverless you only pay for the compute you actually use.

You also get built‑in scaling, so spikes in traffic won’t choke the system.

Practical tip: start by moving a small, high‑frequency table into Fabric’s PostgreSQL.

Validate that query performance meets your SLA,
then expand.

If you’re already on Fabric, enable the PostgreSQL endpoint and point your BI tools at it.

The result is a tighter loop between transactions and insights.

Think of it as collapsing the gap between operational and analytical workloads.

news_posts.post_content:
When you layer specialized AI agents onto a general‑purpose chatbot, the first thing to sort out is how the two systems share data and control.

Adobe has just embedded its CX AI agents into ChatGPT, and Google’s Gemini is being positioned as a competitor for marketing teams. (source: BigGo Finance)

The underlying idea is simple: an agent is a narrow‑purpose model that calls a larger language model for language generation, while the larger model handles conversation flow. The agent owns the business rules, the LLM provides the natural language.

A practical checklist for adding an agent to an existing chatbot:

1. Define the exact task the agent will own (e.g., product recommendation).
2. Map the data it needs and the APIs it will call.
3. Set guardrails – content policies, privacy limits, and fallback triggers.
4. Instrument logging for both agent decisions and LLM outputs.
5. Run a limited pilot and monitor cost, latency, and user satisfaction.

Fact: Adobe’s CX agents now run inside OpenAI’s ChatGPT environment. Interpretation: marketers will have to decide whether a single integrated model or a modular agent‑plus‑LLM stack best fits their workflow.

My recommendation is to start with a single, well‑scoped agent, keep the data pipeline transparent, and expand only after you have measurable KPIs.

concept_posts.post_content:
Imagine a retail data warehouse that stores customer records.

A customer named Alice signs up with address 123 Main St,
 and we load that row into the dimension table.

A month later Alice moves to 456 Oak Ave,
 and we receive an update.

If we simply overwrite the old row,
 we lose the history of where she lived before.

That’s where Slowly Changing Dimensions,
 or SCDs, come in.

SCD Type 1 overwrites the existing value,
 useful when history isn’t needed.

SCD Type 2 adds a new row with start and end dates,
 preserving every change.

SCD Type 3 keeps a limited history by adding extra columns for the previous value.

Key points:

- Choose Type 1 for corrections,
 not for tracking changes.

- Use Type 2 when you need a full audit trail of attribute changes.

- Type 3 is handy for “current vs previous” comparisons without blowing up row count.

A common mistake is mixing Type 1 and Type 2 logic in the same pipeline,
 which leads to duplicate rows or lost history.

Rule of thumb:
 decide early which attributes need full history and implement the matching SCD type consistently.

concept_posts.post_content:
A frequent mistake is leaving the default WAL settings unchanged in a production database.

It means the system may write too much data to disk,
 causing I/O spikes during peak traffic.

To keep things smooth,
 I like to run through a short checklist before I go live.

Here are the three settings I always verify:

- wal_level set to replica so logical decoding works and standby servers can stream.

- max_wal_size tuned to match your storage and workload,
 preventing frequent checkpoints.

- checkpoint_timeout set low enough to avoid long pauses,
 but not so low that it hurts throughput.

One easy trap is to increase max_wal_size without also adjusting checkpoint_completion_target,
 which can delay recovery after a crash.

Make sure you test the configuration with a realistic load before you flip the switch.

Rule of thumb: keep checkpoint intervals under 5 minutes and monitor pg_wal size daily.

Does your current setup follow a similar checklist?
